title: The game of chicken and Scarborough
primary_topics: The South China Sea and East China Sea as theaters of a superpower 'game of chicken' that could ignite a nuclear holocaust
Scenario analysis: what should the Philippines do if China builds a military base on Scarborough Shoal, and how would the US respond?
The Arbitral Award's classification of Scarborough as a 'high-tide elevation' with a 12-NM territorial sea boring a hole in the PH 200-NM EEZ
Noynoy Aquino's rule-of-law arbitration choice as the strategic decision that now even the US uses to support its FONOPs
Author's prescription: pursue the Philippines' own destiny grounded in the rule of law to avoid being an 'expendable pawn' in the international chess game
sub_topics: US 'freedom of navigation' operations using aircraft carriers, warships, submarines, and warplanes despite being a non-signatory to UNCLOS

Allies sending naval and air assets: UK (HMS Queen Elizabeth -- described by British Ambassador Daniel Pruce as 'the largest and most powerful surface vessel in the Royal Navy's history'), Australia, Japan, Germany, France
US silent disregard of its 'one-China policy' through Taiwan arms sales and high-official visits -- driven in part by Taiwan's chip dominance (AI, high-value computing, military software)
China's air-and-naval response: pilots close enough to see each other's digital helmets; warplanes and drones defying Taiwan's ADIZ; Taiwan's ultra-modern US-made jets chasing them
Senkaku Isles (Diaoyu) -- unpopulated, historically claimed by China -- treated by the US as integral parts of Japan such that a Chinese takeover would activate the US-Japan Mutual Defense Treaty
US Seventh Fleet presence in Tokyo Bay
US ~30,000 troops and several bases in South Korea, partly to confront North Korea (China's ally) and partly to contain China's land expansion
Past Scarborough confrontation: US-mediated mutual withdrawal proposal; PH withdrew; China did not and tightened its grip; US did nothing
Aquino factional dissension referenced in Justice Antonio T. Carpio's last column

AA's Scarborough ruling: 'high tide elevation' with a 12-NM territorial sea (24 NM in diameter) carving a hole in the PH 200-NM EEZ -- if China completes occupation, it could exercise sovereignty over the territorial sea and 'shoo away everyone'
Decisive question: is it in US national interest to defend the shoal and risk nuclear war? US has retreated from chicken before
signature_phrases: a dangerous game that could ignite a nuclear holocaust
we should pursue our own destiny and continue to lean on the rule of law
we would not be just another expendable pawn in the old power game of chess of the international masters
the US did nothing. But we did what was best for us
shoo away everyone from the area

stances.claim: The SCS and ECS have become superpower playgrounds for a game of chicken — US-led FONOPs and allied deployments versus China's armada and air sorties — that risks a nuclear holocaust.
stances.evidence: Catalogue of US/UK (HMS Queen Elizabeth)/Australia/Japan/Germany/France deployments; Chinese counter-deployments; Senkaku flashpoint; ADIZ confrontations

stances.claim: The US's response in any future Scarborough-base scenario is uncertain because it has retreated before — past confrontation showed US mediation that left China tightening its grip after PH withdrawal, while the US did nothing.
stances.evidence: Past Scarborough mediation outcome; US's interest-based decision-making

stances.claim: Despite the US's inaction in the past Scarborough confrontation, Noynoy Aquino's rule-of-law arbitration choice was the right path — and now even the US uses the resulting Arbitral Award to support its own actions.
stances.rhetorical_move: vindication-by-uptake: the AA as strategic asset used even by non-signatories
stances.evidence: AA's role in US FONOPs justification; Aquino's choice over factional dissension noted in Carpio's last column

stances.claim: Regardless of what the US or China will do to uphold its own national interests, the Philippines should pursue its own destiny and continue to lean on the rule of law — the only way to avoid being an 'expendable pawn' in the international chess game.
stances.evidence: FLP creed (might-of-being-right); past success of arbitration; risk-asymmetry of relying on US national-interest calculation

notable_anecdotes: British Ambassador Daniel Pruce's description of the HMS Queen Elizabeth as 'the largest and most powerful surface vessel in the Royal Navy's history' — used as evidence of British naval re-engagement in Asia.
Pilots close enough to 'see each other's digital helmets' as a vivid image of how close to actual combat the SCS/ECS confrontations have come.
Past Scarborough confrontation: US mediation, PH withdrew, China did not (despite reportedly agreeing), US did nothing — the column's pivotal cautionary story about relying on US help.

Noynoy Aquino, despite internal factional dissension (referenced in Carpio's last column), choosing arbitration and the rule of law — and the US now using that very Arbitral Award to justify its own FONOPs.
Twin metaphors closing the column: game of chicken (escalation risk) and chess (expendable-pawn risk).

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that the South China Sea and East China Sea have become the playgrounds of a dangerous superpower game of chicken that could ignite a nuclear holocaust. He catalogues US FONOPs (aircraft carriers, warships, submarines, warplanes) -- justified by the Arbitral Award even though the US is neither a party nor a UNCLOS signatory -- and allied deployments (UK's HMS Queen Elizabeth, described by Ambassador Daniel Pruce as 'the largest and most powerful surface vessel in the Royal Navy's history,' plus Australia, Japan, Germany, France). The US sells arms and sends officials to Taiwan in silent disregard of its 'one-China policy' partly because Taiwan hosts the world's biggest and most advanced chip maker whose products feed AI, high-value computing, and military software. China responds with its own armada, jets close enough for pilots to see each other's digital helmets, drones defying Taiwan's ADIZ, periodic sorties near the Senkakus (Diaoyu) -- which the US treats as integral Japanese territory under the US-Japan Mutual Defense Treaty backed by the Seventh Fleet in Tokyo Bay -- and pressure points around the ~30,000 US troops in South Korea. For the Philippines, the operative question is what to do if China builds a Spratly-style military base on Scarborough Shoal, and whether the US will help the way it has helped Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. He recalls the past Scarborough confrontation: the US tried to mediate mutual withdrawal, the Philippines complied, China did not and tightened its grip, and the US did nothing. Yet, despite internal factional dissension narrated in Justice Antonio T. Carpio's last column, former President Noynoy Aquino chose the rule of law and won the Arbitral Award -- which ruled Scarborough a 'high-tide elevation' with a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea boring a hole in the PH 200-NM EEZ -- an award now even the US invokes. He closes that the real question is whether it is in US national interest to defend the shoal and risk nuclear war (it has retreated from chicken before), and that 'in my humble opinion, regardless of what the US (or China) will do to uphold its national interests, we should pursue our own destiny and continue to lean on the rule of law' so the Philippines is not 'just another expendable pawn in the old power game of chess of the international masters.'
